nodes.label: Spec 0003: A new project from the foundation: product identity in two files, one init command, updates by merge (Proposed)
Premise: four coupled decisions in one spec (which names change, how a copy is made, what happens to inherited records, how updates arrive)
nodes.rationale: Each decision constrains the others and a split would let them drift. The risk is building update machinery before any product exists, so the spec decides only what cannot be changed cheaply after the first product starts and builds only what the first derivation calls. The first derived product is the real caller ADR 0001 asks for; the command that takes a later foundation release is described, not built.

nodes.label: Force: the two apps disagree on their own identity, and the Android ID is not in reverse DNS form
Force: identity is spread over files the foundation keeps editing (App.xcconfig, Project.xcconfig, project.pbxproj, app/build.gradle.kts, res/values/app.xml)
Force: two copies of the foundation carry the same ID, so one installs over the other
Force: a copy inherits claims it never earned (the verification record and the scope index name a hosted run in the foundation repository)
Force: the knowledge graph is tied to this checkout (74 tracked cache files under a path-named folder, one owner specific string)
Force: foundation fixes must reach products (a fix typed again in each product will not be applied)
Force: stable names make a merge clean (31 code and config files and 13 paths carry the foundation name)
Force: shared/config/README.md keeps bundle and application IDs in Xcode or Gradle, not in the shared config schema
Force: one maintainer, and real caller first (R8): an unchecked step rests on one person and no tool may exist before something calls it
Without a decision the first product would be renamed by search and replace, differing from the next product in ways nobody chose
User stories: one command names a clone, foundation releases arrive by merge, the verification record lists only what ran here, every push proves the command still works
AC-1: both apps carry the same default identity, read from Identity.xcconfig and identity.properties, stated nowhere else under apps/
AC-2: with the default identity scripts/test.sh passes, both apps build and the greeting tests pass in both appearances
AC-3: init-project.sh --name --app-id writes name, ID, version 0.1.0 and build 1 into both identity files, with per-value overrides
AC-4: the write set is exactly the two identity files, README.md, the verification record and the removed graphify-out/ files; nothing is renamed
AC-5: the verification record becomes the empty record naming the product, foundation URL and revision, with every target unverified
AC-6: README.md has the product name as title on line 1 and the origin line on line 3 followed by one blank line
AC-7: the command refuses, changes nothing and exits 2 with a one line reason (bad input, default ID, dirty tree, derived or mixed checkout, missing foundation URL or ref)
AC-8: init-project.sh --check prints foundation or derived and exits 0, exits 1 naming each mismatch in a mixed state; scripts/test.sh runs it
AC-9: init-project.sh --test runs the unit tests including the derivation on a temporary copy; scripts/test.sh runs it so the foundation CI job proves the command on every push
AC-10: the workflow accepts a manual run with the derived input, and every native job compares the built app's ID and display name with the identity file
AC-11: README.md has a section with the full path from clone to first results, path ownership, taking a later release and foundation tagging
AC-12: docs/scope/index.md no longer links a hosted run, and the ownership matrix, repository structure, quality checks table and shared/config/README.md name the identity files or the command
Option 1 (chosen): clone and merge, product identity in two files, one init command
nodes.rationale: Pros: a foundation release reaches a product by git merge with conflicts only where the product changed the same lines; the changing surface is two files so the command and its check stay small; the Xcode project, scheme and build scripts are never rewritten. Cons: foundation names stay visible in product code; a product carries the foundation's commit history; a command and its tests are kept for a job that runs once per product.

nodes.label: Option 2 (rejected): template copy with a full rename and a fresh history
nodes.rationale: Pros: no trace of the foundation name and a clean history. Cons: unrelated histories mean a foundation fix is moved by hand as a patch per product; the rename must rewrite project.pbxproj, the scheme, the validator constants, both generators and the bindings, each of which can break in a way only a native build shows; the script grows with every name the foundation adds.

nodes.label: Option 3 (rejected): a written checklist, no command
nodes.rationale: Pros: nothing to build, test or keep running, and it fits the rule that a tool needs a caller. Cons: each product is renamed slightly differently and a missed step shows up late; nothing tells a contributor whether a checkout is fully derived; the list goes stale silently when the foundation moves a value.

nodes.label: Decision: a product is a clone that changes only its display name, application ID and version through scripts/init-project.sh, keeps every other name, starts with an empty verification record and merges foundation-v tags
nodes.rationale: The number of products settles it. With one product a checklist would do; with several, the cost that repeats is every later foundation fix, and only a shared history and stable names make that a merge, the one update path a single maintainer will keep using. Renaming everything remains possible later inside one product at the price of leaving the merge path; the reverse move is not possible, which is why the narrow choice comes first.

nodes.label: The narrow choice comes first: a full rename stays possible later inside one product, the reverse move does not
nodes.rationale: The engineer first chose to rename every name (Option 2), then chose product identity only once the conflict with merging was laid out. Leaving the merge path is reversible in one direction only.

nodes.label: One name and one application ID as input
nodes.rationale: The same ID is used on both platforms, with an override per platform for a product that already has different IDs in the stores.

nodes.label: Inherited scope rows and specs stay as history
nodes.rationale: The evidence is what gets emptied: the verification record and the hosted run link.

nodes.label: The Linux proof runs on every push; the native proof runs by hand before a foundation tag
nodes.rationale: scripts/test.sh does not read the application ID, so only a native build tests a changed identity, and that cost is paid once per release.

nodes.label: The Linux proof is one unit test, not a second run of scripts/test.sh
nodes.rationale: A cross check showed that a full second run doubles the lint, the tests and a UniFFI compile while proving almost nothing new, since those steps never read the identity. A --self-test form that ran everything in a copy was the runner up.

nodes.label: Every native run compares the built app with the identity file
nodes.rationale: The greeting tests never read the ID, so without that comparison a run under the sample identity would pass even if the build ignored the identity file.

nodes.label: Only identifiers follow a rename, never prose
nodes.rationale: With product identity only, no document needs rewriting. The one README command that names the ID reads it from the identity file.

nodes.label: No References section
nodes.rationale: Every decision in the spec rests on the repository itself.

nodes.label: Recommendation: one identity file per platform that the foundation never edits again
nodes.rationale: Git reports a conflict when two sides change neighbouring lines, and identity lines inside Project.xcconfig or build.gradle.kts sit next to lines the foundation will change. Editing the values in place was the runner up.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the identity files stay native
nodes.rationale: shared/config/README.md keeps application IDs in Xcode or Gradle. One shared file read by both builds was the runner up; it would break that rule and tie the two platforms together.

nodes.label: Recommendation: Python under tooling/derive/ with a shell entry in scripts/
nodes.rationale: This is the shape the generators already use: Python 3.9 with the standard library only and no new dependency. A pure shell script was the runner up and lost on input checks and tests.

nodes.label: Recommendation: --check accepts two states, foundation and derived
nodes.rationale: One check then runs unchanged in both repositories and catches a half finished derivation in either. A check that passes only after derivation was the runner up and would fail in the foundation itself.

nodes.label: Recommendation: --check does not look for hosted run links
nodes.rationale: The command writes the record from a template, so the record is right by construction. A link test would depend on the exact spelling of a URL and on a file that /scope rewrites.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the command refuses to run on a derived checkout
nodes.rationale: A second run would wipe the product's own verification record. A later change of name or ID is an edit of the two identity files.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the command does not edit scope rows
nodes.rationale: /scope owns those files (spec 0002), and a second writer would break when their shape changes. Marking inherited rows 'existing' is one step in the written path.

nodes.label: Recommendation: after derivation the product owns docs/scope/, docs/specs/ and the verification record
nodes.rationale: On a later merge the product keeps its own side of those paths. No rule file links to a numbered row or spec, so nothing dangles. Sharing one numbering sequence with the foundation was the runner up and collides on the first row either side adds.

nodes.label: Recommendation: the origin line records where a product started and never changes
nodes.rationale: Later releases are visible in git log --merges. Rewriting the line on each merge was the runner up and would make the word 'started' untrue.

nodes.label: Recommendation: tags are named foundation-vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
nodes.rationale: The prefix keeps them apart from a product's own release tags in the same clone. A plain v prefix was the runner up.

nodes.label: Recommendation: no changelog file and no sync command yet
nodes.rationale: Tags and a path limited git log give the list of changes for one maintainer. Both get built when the first foundation release is merged into a product, which is their real caller.

nodes.label: apps/ios/Config/Identity.xcconfig (iOS identity file: APP_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER, APP_DISPLAY_NAME, MARKETING_VERSION, CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION)
apps/android/identity.properties (Android identity file: applicationId, displayName, versionName, versionCode)
scripts/init-project.sh (init command with --name/--app-id, --check and --test forms)
tooling/derive/init_project.py (derivation logic, input checks and the default application ID constant)
tooling/derive/test_init_project.py (unit tests for the init command, including the derivation case)
tooling/derive/verification-record.md (empty verification record template)
Product identity data model: application ID, display name, version and build in two identity files, one origin line, two repository states
Default foundation identity: dev.foundation.mobile, Mobile Foundation, version 0.1.0, build 1
Input validation rules (re.ASCII patterns for app ID, platform overrides, display name of 1 to 30 code points, version, build, foundation URL, ref and date)
iOS build reads Identity.xcconfig: Project.xcconfig includes it, App.xcconfig maps the bundle ID and display name, the UI test bundle ID is derived as $(APP_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER).uitests

Android build reads identity.properties: app/build.gradle.kts loads applicationId, versionName and versionCode, the label reaches the manifest as the appLabel placeholder, namespace stays foundation.mobile

Names the foundation keeps: MobileFoundation project, targets and scheme, rootProject.name, crates foundation-core and mobile-ffi, mobile_ffi namespace, Kotlin packages, FoundationTokens, FoundationTheme, foundation_strings.xml, foundation.json, the workflow file
nodes.rationale: Stable names are what make a later foundation merge clean, so no product changes them; only the display name, application ID and version are product identity.

nodes.label: README origin line on line 3: Started from the [mobile foundation](<URL>) at `<ref>` on <date>.
Empty verification record: names the product, foundation URL and ref, lists every target as still unverified, holds no hosted run link
Repository states: foundation (both IDs default, no origin line), derived (neither ID default, valid origin line), mixed (anything else)
Init write set: the two identity files, the README title and origin line, the empty verification record and the removal of graphify-out/
init-project.sh --check: prints foundation or derived (exit 0) or names each mismatch in a mixed state (exit 1)
init-project.sh --test: runs the unit tests under tooling/derive/

Derivation test: copies the files git lists to a temporary folder, runs the copy's own command with sample values, requires --check to print derived and check-architecture.py to pass, then removes the copy
Refusals: one line naming the input and the rule, exit 2, nothing written
Safe write order: nothing is written until every check passes, contents are built in memory, each file moves into place with os.replace, graphify-out/ is removed last, git restore . is the way back
Sample values: --name "Zoë's Proof" --app-id dev.example.derived, foundation URL https://example.invalid/foundation, ref foundation-v0.0.0, date 2026-01-01
nodes.rationale: The name carries a letter outside ASCII and an apostrophe on purpose. If the Android build rejects or alters the apostrophe, the apostrophe is removed from the name rule in the same change rather than adding escaping.

nodes.label: Unit tests create their own repository in a temporary folder with isolated git configuration; no test touches the real checkout

Foundation URL sourcing and normalization: --foundation-url, else the foundation remote, else origin; https, http, ssh and user@host:path forms written as https without user, token, .git or trailing slash
Foundation ref resolution: --foundation-ref, else the highest foundation-v* tag exactly at HEAD, else the full HEAD commit ID
CI identity comparison: each native job compares the built app's ID and display name (PlistBuddy on Info.plist, aapt2 dump badging on the debug APK) with its identity file and fails on a difference
Workflow input derived (workflow_dispatch boolean): the ios and android jobs run the command on the runner checkout, then build and test under the sample identity

Key invariants: a checkout is foundation or derived, each identity value has one home per platform, the command renames nothing, never runs on a derived or mixed checkout, never changes git state, and foundation tags match foundation-v*

Security model: reads and writes only inside the checkout, no network and no secret, credentials stripped from the remote URL, inputs checked before any write, signing material stays out of the repository (R12)
Build plan: eleven steps, one thin thread first (identity from its file through each build into the running app), then the command, then the proofs and the written path

Document updates (step 10): scope index, ownership matrix row for product identity, repository structure, architecture compliance row for project identity state, shared/config/README.md, spec 0001 rule R1 (ten to eleven)

README section 'Start a project from this foundation': clone at a tag, create a branch, rename the remote, run the command, add origin, rebuild the graph, mark inherited rows existing, commit, record first results
Path ownership after derivation: product owned paths keep the product's side, foundation owned paths take the foundation's side, shared paths merge by hand
Take a later foundation release: git fetch foundation --tags, git merge foundation-vX.Y.Z, keep the product's side on product owned paths, rebuild the graph, run every check
Release the foundation: run the workflow by hand with derived set, then push an annotated foundation-vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tag on main

Positive: products install side by side under their own name and ID, a foundation fix reaches every product by one merge, a half derived checkout fails scripts/test.sh, records start empty, the identity mismatch is gone, every native run proves the built identity
Tradeoff: foundation names stay in product code (MobileFoundation project, scheme and bundle, Foundation-prefixed types and packages); users see only the display name
Tradeoff: a product carries the foundation's commit history and its foundation-v tags
Tradeoff: a command and its unit tests are kept for a job that runs once per product
Tradeoff: the Linux proof builds nothing, so a change that breaks a derived native build can sit on main until the next manual derived run
Tradeoff: rebuilding the graph, marking inherited rows existing and recording the first results rest on the person; --check does not see them
Tradeoff: every merge of a foundation release reports conflicts on product owned paths, resolved by hand until the sync command exists
Tradeoff: later foundation scope rows and specs do not flow into products; the reason behind a new foundation rule is read in the foundation repository
Tradeoff: display names are limited to letters, digits, space, period, hyphen and apostrophe until a product needs more
Tradeoff: the Android application ID changes from foundation.mobile to dev.foundation.mobile, leaving an old debug build as a separate app
Neutral: the ownership matrix grows to eleven rows and spec 0001 is amended in the same change
Neutral: the iOS version moves from 1.0 to 0.1.0 to match Android; the Cargo workspace version is not an app version and is left alone
Neutral: /develop moves the spec to In Progress and Accepted with scope row 009; creating the first tag foundation-v0.1.0 is the maintainer's step
Follow-up: build the command that takes a foundation release (fetch, merge, apply the ownership table) when the first release is merged into a product
Follow-up: write how a change proven in a product returns to the foundation once a product closes a Deferred item
Follow-up: record where /graphify and /scope come from, with a way to do each step by hand
Follow-up: decide where dependency update bots run (a bot in every product changes foundation owned files and will conflict with merges)
Follow-up: two foundation schemas still require sample names (greeting_recipient, the greeting role); this deserves its own scope row
Follow-up: decide in the release path spec whether the iOS and Android versions must match, and add that test to --check if they must
Follow-up: allow a localized display name when a product needs one (it would move from the identity files to the catalogs)
Follow-up: revisit keeping MobileFoundation as the Xcode project and scheme name if it confuses contributors to a product
ADR 0001: Native apps with a shared Rust core
Spec 0001: One owner per responsibility, with rules kept beside the code
Spec 0002: One planning path: a scope row first, then a spec
R8: real caller first (a service, adapter, view model or capability interface needs an actual caller; smallest slice its caller can exercise)
R1: each responsibility has one authoritative owner (the matrix lists ten)
R12: binaries, signing material, SDK paths and IDE data stay out; compiler and dependencies pinned, builds use --locked
Force: one maintainer, so no second reviewer by default
Follow-up: record where /scope and /architect come from when a second contributor joins
